title: The blueprint (Genesis Rabbah 1:1)
hookLine: God looked into the Torah and made the world, like an architect with plans
tomorrow: if God had a blueprint, why tear worlds down?

cards: Nobody pours a foundation and then asks where the stairs go. Before one shovel hits the dirt, somebody has drawn the whole house: every door, every outlet, which way the windows face. Genesis opens on a much bigger build.
"In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." One line, and a world is standing. No sketch, no plans on the table.
The rabbis of the midrash read that line slowly and asked the builder's question: built from what?

teach.b: Genesis Rabbah starts its answer in the book of Proverbs. There, wisdom speaks, and the rabbis hear the Torah's own voice in it: "Then I was by Him, as a nursling; and I was daily all delight."
The Hebrew word behind nursling is amon, and the midrash reads it several ways: a nursling, a tutor, something hidden, something great. And one more: uman, an artisan.

teach.h: THE TORAH: I WAS THE TOOL.
teach.b: Then the Torah speaks for itself: I was the craftsman's tool. Here comes the parable. When a human king builds a palace, he doesn't build from his own head.
He calls an architect. And the architect doesn't build from his own head either: he has plans and notebooks, to know where the rooms go and where the doors open.
So too, the midrash says, the Holy One looked into the Torah and created the world. Notice what that does.
In this reading the Torah isn't only a book that arrives later, at Sinai, with instructions stuck onto a finished world. It was there first, as the drawing the world was built from.
So a law about rest on the seventh day, or leaving the corner of a field for the hungry, isn't a fence added afterward. It's the plan, read back.
And the midrash ties it to the very first word, in the beginning, because Proverbs has wisdom say God made her as the beginning of His way.

how: Genesis Rabbah 1:1 is often studied at the start of the yearly Torah reading cycle, when Genesis begins again in synagogues on the Sabbath after Simchat Torah.

games.q: your group is building a parade float. half want to start gluing now; you're holding the sketch. by the midrash's parable, what comes first?
o: the sketch: even the king's architect works from plans.
start gluing; the plan will show up as you go.
skip it; a great builder keeps it all in their head.
games.why: in Genesis Rabbah even the king doesn't build from his own head. the architect has plans, and God looked into the Torah.

practice: Pick one thing you'll build tomorrow, something small: a meal, a hard conversation, a page of work. For this sit, draw it in your head the way an architect would: where it starts, what it needs, where the door is if it goes wrong.
No building yet, just the plan, held still.

wordCard.voice: The blueprint: in Genesis Rabbah, the Torah as the plan God looked into before building the world. The drawing came first.

orig.note: Hebrew: the word in Proverbs 8:30 that Genesis Rabbah reads as uman, an artisan.
